name: Dead-Letter Queues and Poison Messages
intent: Give messages that can never be processed a bounded number of retries and then a place to wait for a human, so one bad message cannot block or burn the queue.
scenario: An order-processing queue where 2% of messages have a bad address field. The worker cannot build a shipping label for them, so each one fails every time it is delivered, and the orders behind it in the same partition wait.
problem: A queue with at-least-once delivery redelivers any message that is not acknowledged. That is exactly right for a crashed worker or a timeout, and exactly wrong for a poison message: a malformed payload, a bug triggered by one input, or a reference to something that no longer exists. It fails on every attempt, so it is redelivered forever. In an ordered queue or a partition it blocks everything behind it (head-of-line blocking); in an unordered queue it keeps a worker busy for nothing. Four poison messages in a 4-worker pool can stop the whole pool while healthy messages age.

howItWorks.title: Count deliveries and set a limit
howItWorks.text: The broker or the consumer counts how many times a message was delivered (SQS ApproximateReceiveCount with a redrive policy maxReceiveCount, RabbitMQ x-delivery-count on quorum queues, a retry counter in a header for Kafka). When the count passes the limit, typically 3 to 10, the message is no longer retried in place. Without a limit, retry forever is the default behaviour of most brokers.

howItWorks.title: Park it in a dead-letter queue with its context
howItWorks.text: The message goes to a separate queue or topic (the DLQ) that no worker reads automatically. Keep the original body plus metadata: the last error and stack trace, attempt count, original queue or topic, partition and offset, first-failed and last-failed timestamps. A bare payload with no error is hard to diagnose. Kafka has no built-in DLQ: the consumer publishes to a dead-letter topic itself.

howItWorks.title: Separate transient from permanent errors
howItWorks.text: Retry a timeout, a 503 or a lock conflict, because trying again can work. Do not retry a validation error, a failed deserialisation or a 404 for a referenced row, because it cannot. Sending permanent errors straight to the DLQ on the first attempt saves the wasted retries and gets the queue moving sooner. When unsure, retry a few times and then park.

howItWorks.title: Retry transient failures with delays
howItWorks.text: Instant retries just hammer a dependency that is down. Retry with growing delays (for example 1 s, 10 s, 1 min) using delay features (SQS delay or visibility timeout, RabbitMQ dead-letter exchange with TTL) or retry topics with increasing delays in Kafka. This frees the main queue, but the message now re-enters later and may be processed after messages that came after it.

howItWorks.title: Alarm on the DLQ, then fix and redrive
howItWorks.text: A DLQ nobody watches is a silent data-loss mechanism. Alarm on depth above 0 and on the age of the oldest message, and set retention longer than the on-call response time (SQS allows up to 14 days). After fixing the bug or the data, redrive the messages back to the source queue (SQS has a redrive-to-source action). Redriven messages can run a second time or out of order, so the handler must be idempotent.

pros: One bad message can no longer block a partition or burn all the workers
Failed messages are kept with their error, so a fix can be followed by a replay instead of data loss
Retry limits bound the wasted work and the load on a struggling dependency
Depth and age of the DLQ give a clear, cheap signal that something is wrong with the data or the code
cons: Someone must own the DLQ: alarms, triage, redrive, and a decision about messages that can never be fixed
Parking a message in an ordered stream lets later messages for the same key overtake it, so per-key order can break
A limit set too low parks healthy messages during a short outage; too high wastes work and delays the queue
The DLQ holds raw payloads, often personal data, with its own retention and access needs
Redriving needs idempotent handlers and care not to loop a still-broken message back into the DLQ
whenToUse: Any queue or topic with at-least-once delivery and a consumer that can fail on specific inputs
Pipelines where losing a message is worse than delaying it: orders, payments, events that update other systems
Ordered partitions where one bad record would otherwise stall every record behind it
Systems with input you do not fully control, such as user data, third-party webhooks or old messages in a schema that has since changed
whenNotToUse: Best-effort or disposable messages (metrics samples, cache invalidations) where dropping after a few tries is fine and a DLQ nobody reads is just clutter
As a replacement for validating input at the producer: bad data should be rejected at the edge when possible
As a place to hide an outage: if every message is landing in the DLQ the dependency is down, which is a circuit breaker or backpressure problem
Strictly ordered pipelines that cannot tolerate a gap; there you block the key and page someone rather than skip the message
pitfalls: An ignored DLQ: messages pile up with no alarm until retention deletes them, which is silent data loss with extra steps
Retrying permanent errors (a 400, a deserialisation exception) up to the limit, wasting attempts and delaying the whole queue
A retry limit of 1 or 2 during a brief outage parks thousands of healthy messages at once; count only errors you know are the message's fault, or make the limit generous
Setting the queue's message retention shorter than the DLQ alarm response time, so messages expire in the DLQ before anyone looks
Redriving without idempotency: a message that half-succeeded before failing is applied twice
Redriving everything at full speed into a system that has just recovered, which causes a second outage; throttle the redrive
Putting full payloads with personal data (names, addresses, card fragments) in a DLQ with wider access or longer retention than the source queue
Skipping a poison message in a keyed stream and moving on, so a later update for the same order is applied before the earlier one that is now in the DLQ

roles.label: Queue
roles.description: Stores messages, counts deliveries and redelivers anything not acknowledged.

roles.label: Consumer
roles.description: Processes one message at a time and acknowledges it on success.

roles.label: Dead-letter queue
roles.description: Holds messages that exceeded the retry limit, with their error and attempt count.

roles.label: Operator
roles.description: Gets the alarm, inspects parked messages, fixes the cause and redrives.
